Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
628 PM EST Wed Nov 11 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 242 PM EST Wednesday...

A Winter Weather Advisory has been issued for the higher terrain
of the Adirondacks and portions of the southern Green Mountains
for Thursday and early Friday.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 242 PM EST Wednesday...

1. A coastal low will bring widespread lower elevation rain and
wet snow mainly above 1200 feet with shower chances continuing
through the weekend. 

2. A few lingering showers Sunday, then high confidence in dry 
weather early next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 242 PM EST Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Model consensus continues to favor a coastal type
low to deepen and wrap moisture back across Vermont and northern
New York Thursday with a more upslope regime developing by
Friday. Temperatures and this pattern support lower elevation
rain Thursday and mainly higher elevation snowfall before
temperatures drop Thursday night promoting snow showers to most
valley floors. The overall forecast remains quite tricky with
balancing QPF timing, changing SLRs, and a shift in primary
precipitation mechanisms while models struggle with the details.

Where the models continue to struggle are placement of the
surface circulation, extent of northward moisture transport and
QPF amounts, and amount of cold air in place across the region.
The latest trends have pushed moisture back southward leaving
more modest QPF across northern New York and Vermont
representing nearly a 50% reduction to QPF from the previous
forecast for many locations. As such, snow totals were decreased
with most spots only seeing a dusting to around 1 inch, southern
and Adirondack locations below 1200 feet receiving 1-2 inches,
and 2-5 inches above 1200ft. This will primarily be a function
of the period of heaviest precipitation period occurring over 
the daytime hours with snow ratios being lower due to thermal 
profiles. As such, snow will start at higher elevations and 
crash down to around 1000 feet over the evening hours as the low
pulls away. The upslope regime begins Thursday night and 
continues through early Friday with higher snow ratios 
supporting more efficient accumulation rates, but hindered by 
decreasing moisture. Cooling profiles and dynamic cooling 
processes will help snow reach most valley locations overnight 
Thursday night and early Friday. However, it will be tough to 
get snow accumulations in lower valleys like the Champlain 
Valley given the relatively warm ground temperatures likely 
melting most, if not all, of the snow that reaches the ground 
Thursday night. For the St Lawrence Valley, most of the moisture
will have exited before temperature profiles cool enough to 
allow snow to occur. 

Behind the coastal low, northerly flow will remain through
Saturday keeping shower chances ongoing, especially across
terrain. One "gotcha" to watch out for will be the potential for
streamers to form off of Lake Champlain producing some higher
elevation snow showers. Temperatures over the weekend may be
cooler as well depending on cloud cover which may keep highs
lower. Valley highs over the weekend are favored in the lower
40s, but could decrease into the upper 30s if clouds proliferate
off of Lake Champlain given continued cool air advection. Lows
will be in the 20s for most spots. 

KEY MESSAGE 2:  The departing low will continue to pull away from the 
region Sunday, leading to continued northwesterly wrap-around flow 
with a few lingering showers.  As the low exits, the depth of 
moisture will decrease throughout the day and shower coverage will 
further decrease from Saturday. Lower elevations will be mostly dry, 
while higher elevations Sunday will still see a few showers. 
Throughout the weekend, precipitation type will be elevation-
dependent; snow levels will be generally between 1000 and 1500 ft. 
Higher elevations will pick up up to an additional inch over the 
weekend, with limited depth of moisture being the main limiting 
factor in larger wrap-around snow accumulations. Lower elevations 
should not expect any accumulating snow. 

Monday onward, the forecast turns very quiet with high confidence in 
high pressure building in and larger diurnal temperature swings. 
Highs will be near seasonable normals, but lows will be chillier 
than normal, especially going into midweek.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z THURSDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Through 00Z Friday...VFR ceilings will prevail through
midnight, with cloud bases between 3000 and 8000 ft AGL. After 
midnight, ceilings will gradually lower, with ceilings becoming 
predominantly MVFR after 12Z. Rain and snow showers will spread
into the area from southwest to northeast after 12Z Thursday.
Precipitation type will be elevation dependent; snow levels 
will hover between 1000 and 2000 ft. Lowest flight conditions 
in the back half of the TAF period will be at KSLK and KRUT, 
where a trend towards IFR is expected after 12Z as precipitation
and lower ceilings affect these terminals first. Winds will 
generally be light and variable through the next 24 hours. 

Outlook...

Thursday Night: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. Definite RA,
Chance SN.
Friday: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance SN, Chance
RA.
Friday Night: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Slight chance
RA, Slight chance SN.
Saturday: Mainly MVFR, with local VFR possible. Chance RA, Chance
SN.
Saturday Night: Mainly MVFR, with local VFR possible. Chance SN,
Chance RA.
Sunday: MVFR. Chance RA, Chance SN.
Sunday Night: Mainly MVFR, with areas VFR possible. Slight chance
SN.
Monday: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. NO SIG WX.

&&

     Friday for VTZ018-019.
NY...Winter Weather Advisory from 10 AM Thursday to 10 AM EST 
     Friday for NYZ034.
